meta.title: The Street That Had to Be Crossed
meta.skill_frame: Author's craft: read how the writer uses understatement.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fourth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured part_1 114w at FK 5.9, part_2 139w at FK 6.2, part_3 127w at FK 7.2. The load is understatement, short factual sentences, and order of events in a battle account.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.basis: Adapted from Ulysses S. Grant, Personal Memoirs of U. S. Grant, Vol. 1 (1885), under DESIGN_RULES 2.5.
source.attribution: Grant, Ulysses S. Personal Memoirs of U. S. Grant, Vol. 1. 1885. Project Gutenberg eBook #1067, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/1067, accessed 2026-11-11. Public domain in the United States.
source.adaptation: Split long sentences, replaced rare words, removed unit numbers not needed by an item; no facts added.
source.survey: A commander describes a street crossing under fire and the losses it cost.
source.avoided: No invented numbers, names, or outcomes beyond the source.

session.difficulty_basis: understatement, short factual sentences, and order of events in a battle account

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: The streets leading to the plaza were commanded by artillery from all sides; the houses were flat-roofed and one or two stories high. Around the plaza, infantry held the roofs. Sand-bags protected them from our fire. On streets not leading to the plaza, our men were safe from enemy fire and sight, except at crossings; at each crossing they met musket fire and grape-shot. The 3d and 4th regiments advanced nearly to the plaza this way. They lost many men. The regiment had five companies and no more than twelve officers. Five of these officers were killed. We had not held this position long when we found our ammunition was low.
passage.part_2: I volunteered to go back to where we started, report our position to General Twiggs, and ask for ammunition. We were off the street, behind the houses. My ride back was an exposed one. Before starting, I moved to the horse's side away from the enemy, one foot on the cantle, an arm over its neck. I started at full run. My horse was under fire only at street crossings; I crossed these so fast that I was usually past and under cover of the next block before the enemy fired. I got out safely without a scratch. The house was full of wounded American officers and soldiers. I dismounted and went in. I promised to report their situation, left, readjusted myself on my horse, and resumed the run. I was soon with the troops at the east end.
passage.part_3: Before ammunition could be collected, the two regiments I had been with were seen coming back; they ran the same gauntlet getting out as going in, but with little loss; the movement was canceled. The troops were withdrawn. The wounded officers and men I had found fell into enemy hands that night. At the east, General Worth, with a small division of troops, moved toward the plaza from the other end of the city. He got near the plaza that night with little loss of life. Before morning, Ampudia, the Mexican commander, asked to surrender the city and garrison. This stopped all further fighting. The terms of surrender were soon agreed. The prisoners were released on parole. They could take their horses and personal property with them.

items.prompt: What does the writer say the soldiers found about their ammunition?

tutor_only.confirm: They found their ammunition was low.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The last sentence of part 1 states, "We had not held this position long when we found our ammunition was low."
tutor_only.tell: The writer states the ammunition problem in one short sentence. This fact leads to the ride for ammunition later.
help: Look at the final sentence of the opening.
Find the words about ammunition running low.
tutor_only.core_idea: The writer states that ammunition was low.
accept_ideas: They found their ammunition was low.
The soldiers were low on ammunition.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say the soldiers had no ammunition at all.
if_they_say.ask: Does the passage say their ammunition was gone, or low?

items.prompt: The writer says the men were safe on streets that did not lead to the plaza. What happened at the crossings?

tutor_only.confirm: The men were safe on those streets, but at each crossing they met musket fire and grape-shot.
tutor_only.correct_reason: Sentence 4 states both facts: safety from enemy fire and sight on streets not leading to the plaza, and musket fire and grape-shot at each crossing.
tutor_only.tell: The sentence sets safety on those streets against danger at crossings. At each crossing, the men met musket fire and grape-shot.
help: Look at the sentence that begins 'On streets not leading to the plaza.'
Find the word 'except' and the two situations it joins.
tutor_only.core_idea: The sentence connects safety on streets away from the plaza with danger at each crossing.
accept_ideas: Men were safe on streets not leading to the plaza except at crossings.
At each crossing they met musket fire and grape-shot.
The sentence contrasts safety on the streets with danger at the crossings.
They got into fights with the enemy at the crossings.
They fought the enemy at each crossing.
not_required: Naming every weapon in the passage
Explaining where the artillery was placed
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: The student says the men were safe everywhere on those streets.
if_they_say.ask: Which word in the sentence marks the exception?

if_they_say.when: The student says the sentence is only about artillery.
if_they_say.ask: Which weapons does the sentence name at the crossings?

items.prompt: The writer says his horse was under fire at the street crossings. What conclusion about the danger does that detail support but not state?

tutor_only.confirm: The ride was dangerous because enemy fire could reach him at the crossings.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The sentence 'My horse was under fire only at street crossings' shows enemy fire could reach him during the ride, so the facts support danger even though the writer does not state it directly.
tutor_only.tell: The writer says the horse was under fire at street crossings. That detail shows the ride carried danger even though he got out safely.
help: Find the sentence that tells where the horse was under fire.
Notice what the enemy did before he reached the next block.
tutor_only.core_idea: The details of enemy fire at street crossings support the unstated conclusion that the ride was dangerous.
accept_ideas: Enemy fire could reach him at the crossings.
He was at risk of being shot during the ride.
He could have been hit before reaching cover.
not_required: How many wounded men were in the house
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: The student says the ride was safe because he got out without a scratch.
if_they_say.ask: What does the sentence about street crossings say about enemy fire?

if_they_say.when: The student says the horse was never under fire.
if_they_say.ask: Where does the writer say the horse was under fire?

partial.when: The student says he rode fast, crossed before the enemy fired, or got across safely, without saying the ride was dangerous.
partial.ask: What does that show about the danger of the ride?

partial.when: The student says the street-crossing sentence is about the outward ride.
partial.ask: The paragraph begins 'My ride back was an exposed one.' Which ride does the crossing sentence describe?

items.prompt: His horse was under fire, yet he says he came out 'without a scratch'. What does that plain wording do?

tutor_only.confirm: It makes the danger sound smaller than it was. The flat phrase understates the ride.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The passage says the horse was under fire at the crossings, then reports the writer got out 'without a scratch'. The plain phrase plays the danger down.
tutor_only.tell: The horse was under fire, but he says 'without a scratch', so the danger sounds smaller than it was.
help: Look at the sentence about getting out safely.
Notice what 'without a scratch' leaves out about the danger.
tutor_only.core_idea: The flat phrase 'without a scratch' understates the ride: the danger sounds smaller than the fire he describes.
accept_ideas: it makes the danger sound smaller than it was
he downplays how dangerous the ride was
the flat words hide the danger
it makes a ride under fire sound ordinary
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: The student says the phrase proves the ride was not dangerous.
if_they_say.ask: Which sentence says the ride was exposed?

if_they_say.when: The student says "without a scratch" means no one fired at him.
if_they_say.ask: Which sentence says his horse was under fire at crossings?

partial.when: The student says he was not injured, he was safe, or he got back without trouble, without saying what the plain phrase does to the danger.
partial.ask: What does the plain phrase make the danger feel like?

partial.when: the student answers that he was safe, or that he escaped without injury, as the answer
partial.ask: The horse was under fire. What does the phrase 'without a scratch' do to how dangerous that sounds?

items.prompt: How does the writer show the plan changing near the end?

tutor_only.confirm: The writer shows the advance being canceled and the troops withdrawn.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The sentence beginning 'Before ammunition could be collected' states the movement was canceled.
tutor_only.tell: The opening describes the regiments advancing toward the plaza. The last part says the movement was canceled and the troops withdrew.
help: Find the sentence that begins 'Before ammunition could be collected.'
Look for what happens to the movement after the regiments return.
tutor_only.core_idea: The writer shifts from the advance to the canceled movement and withdrawal.
accept_ideas: The writer says the movement was canceled and the troops withdrew.
The advance ends when the regiments are seen coming back.
The plan to keep advancing stops.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say the writer shows the plan succeeding.
if_they_say.ask: Which sentence says the movement was canceled?

if_they_say.when: They say the narrator keeps advancing in part 3.
if_they_say.ask: Which sentence shows the troops were withdrawn?
